items.title: A new validation rule also applies to old backups
items.body:
**Key: backup imports: validateState calls validateItem, so old below-cost backups are now rejected.**

`validateItem` is not only used by the item form. When a backup is imported, the whole state is checked with `validateState`, which runs `s.items.forEach(validateItem)`. So the stricter rule also judges every item in every old backup. A backup that contains a below-cost item, which was valid yesterday, will now be refused. The solutions chapter says to put that in the PR description so reviewers know.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Nothing else, form only*: `validateState` calls `validateItem` for every item.
- *Shipments re-priced*: shipments keep their accepted snapshot; nothing re-prices them.
- *Below-cost items excluded from scoring*: `eligible` checks active, stock and blocked tags only; prices do not affect recommendations.

excerpts.quote: s.items.forEach(validateItem);
Review note: this rule also applies to every backup on import, because `validateState` calls `validateItem`; an old backup with a below-cost item would now be rejected. Say so in the PR.

items.title: Reserve takes one, cancel gives one back, once
items.body:
**Key: 4: reserve takes one, packing none, cancel returns one, and terminal Cancelled blocks a second return.**

Follow the counter. Start at 4. Reserving runs `item.stock--` in the reserve branch: 3. Packing is a transition with no stock code: still 3. Cancelling runs `item.stock++` for each line: back to 4. Could a second cancel add another unit? No: `transitions.Cancelled` is an empty list, so "Cancelled → Cancelled" is not an allowed transition and `reduce` throws.

Why the others are wrong:
- *3, no return after packing*: the guide says cancellation from Reserved *or Packed* returns one per item.
- *4 now, 5 after a second cancel*: Cancelled is terminal; the second transition is refused.
- *2, pack subtracts too*: "Packing does not subtract again."

excerpts.quote: Reserving a box subtracts one from each distinct selected item. Packing does not subtract again. Shipping and delivery retain the deduction. Cancellation from Reserved or Packed returns one per item and becomes terminal, preventing a second return.
if (c.status === "Cancelled") for (const l of sh.quote.lines) { const item = n.items.find((i) => i.id === l.itemId); item.stock++;
Packed: ["Shipped", "Cancelled"], Shipped: ["Delivered"], Delivered: [], Cancelled: [],

items.title: Stock, request keys and frozen receipts
items.body:
Three ideas run through this pack.

- **Available stock.** The `stock` field means units available for new reservations. Learn exactly which shipment steps change it and which do not; the concepts guide spells it out step by step.
- **Two kinds of identity.** A *request key* names one attempt to reserve, so a retry after a network hiccup can find the receipt it already made. A *subscriber-month* (the cycle) names a business slot: one box per subscriber per month. They protect against different kinds of duplicate.
- **Snapshots.** When a box is reserved, the shipment copies the facts it was accepted with (names, prices, costs). Later catalog edits must not rewrite that receipt.

While reading `reduce`, find the `reserve` branch and the `shipment.transition` branch, and note every line that touches `item.stock`.

excerpts.quote: `stock` means units currently available for new reservations.
A request key identifies one attempted reservation command.
Editing the live catalog later must not change those accepted facts.

readMore.why: The worked reservation, reproduced step by step.

items.title: The last-unit loser fails the baseline check, not the stock check
items.body:
**Key: the raw-baseline check in the lock rejects it before reduce sees stock, so unrelated writes conflict too.**

Both tabs loaded the same stored text as their `base`. The winner commits first and the stored text changes. When the loser gets the lock, `commit` reloads storage, `replay` finds nothing (new request key), and then `current.raw !== base.raw` is true, so it throws "Workspace changed in another tab" before `reduce` runs. Because the comparison is on the whole stored text, any accepted write by another tab, even to an unrelated record, causes the same refusal.

Why the others are wrong:
- *replay rejects it*: each attempt has its own request key, and replay only returns a receipt; it is not the check that fails here.
- *Web Locks reject the second tab*: the lock only makes the second tab wait its turn.
- *reduce's stock check rejects it*: the guide says stock "never gets the chance" in this race.

excerpts.quote: if (replay(current.state, command)) return current; if (current.raw !== base.raw) throw new Error( "Workspace changed in another tab. Export your draft and reload before saving.", );
Consequence: any two concurrent writes conflict, even on unrelated records, and the user is asked to reload. Safe, but coarse.

items.title: Start here: ParcelPilot, a subscription-box app in one browser value
items.body:
Buildsubbox runs as ParcelPilot: a local app for managing fictional subscription boxes (items, plans, subscribers, monthly boxes and their shipments). Everything is stored in one localStorage value. The lesson is how to keep an accepted business operation correct while the catalog, the UI and other browser tabs keep changing.

Suggested reading order:

1. `astraupskill/README.md`: what the app does and the learning route.
2. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: trace form input through the repository and the model.
3. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: stock, snapshots, request keys, cycles and concurrency. Most concept quizzes come from here.
4. `src/model.js` (`eligible`, `recommendations`, `replay`, `reduce`) and `src/repository.js` (`commit`, lines 11-24).
5. `astraupskill/05-PRACTICE.md`: nine exercises, each with a Goal and a Check. The goal-check quizzes ask you to match them.
6. `astraupskill/06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`, after you tried the exercises.

The test suite needs only Node 22.12+: `npm test` on a clean tree reports 36 passing tests.

excerpts.quote: The central lesson is preserving an accepted business operation while the catalog, user interface, and other browser tabs keep changing.
A clean tree reports `# tests 36`, `# pass 36`.

readMore.why: The learning route and the junior and mid-level milestones for this workshop.
Where each piece of the app lives and how a save travels to storage.

items.title: Exercise 9's check: HTTP tests with real status codes
items.body:
**Key: "Automated HTTP tests show: unauthenticated inventory edit → 401; two clients racing for the last unit → exactly one 201 ...".**

This is a goal-check question: the practice guide gives each exercise a **Goal** and a **Check**, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

This goal is Exercise 9: rebuild the reservation boundary on a server with authentication, a migration and a test database. Only the matching check talks about HTTP status codes: 401 without login, exactly one 201 when two clients race for the last unit, 409 for a reused key with a different body and for a second request for the same subscriber-month, and 400 with nothing written for invalid input. Those are the server versions of the browser rules you studied.

Why the others do not fit:
- *The `node -e ... recommendations` command*: Exercise 1.
- *Suite still passes, two sentences*: Exercise 4.
- *"# tests 37, # fail 1 ..."*: Exercise 2, the below-cost rule.

excerpts.quote: **Goal.** Rebuild the reservation boundary on a server with real constraints.
same key with a different body → 409; same subscriber and month with a new key → 409; a body failing validation → 400 with nothing written.

readMore.why: What a server must keep from today's commit: lock, replay, base comparison, reduce, write.

items.title: A cancelled month is still taken, whatever the request key
items.body:
**Key: it is refused: the subscriber-month cycle rule still holds after cancellation, whatever the key.**

In the `reserve` branch of `reduce`, the first business check looks for any shipment with the same subscriber and cycle, without looking at status. The cancelled May shipment is still in the list, so the check fails with "This subscriber cycle already has a reservation, including cancelled history." The request key does not matter: it answers "is this a retry of the same attempt?", while the cycle rule answers "is this month's slot free?".

Why the others are wrong:
- *Succeeds with a new key*: the cycle check does not look at keys.
- *Succeeds if fingerprints match*: fingerprints only matter when the same request key is reused.
- *Returns the cancelled shipment*: `replay` matches on the request key, and a brand-new key finds nothing.

excerpts.quote: sh.quote.subscriberId === c.quote.subscriberId && sh.cycle === c.cycle, ), "This subscriber cycle already has a reservation, including cancelled history.",
A new request key cannot create another shipment for that same subscriber-month, even after cancellation.

items.title: Look-then-insert cannot stop two concurrent inserts
items.body:
**Key: two concurrent requests can both see no row and both insert; unique constraints must arbitrate.**

Picture two requests at the same moment. Request A runs the SELECT: no shipment. Request B runs the SELECT: still no shipment, because A has not inserted yet. Now both INSERT, and the subscriber has two boxes for one month. A lookup only tells you what was true a moment ago. The database must enforce the rule itself, with a unique constraint on (subscriber, month) plus proper transaction handling, so that the second insert fails.

Why the others are wrong:
- *SQL cannot store request keys*: a database can store them fine; the guide's point is that you need constraints too.
- *Same HTTP handler is enough*: two handlers for two requests still run at the same time.
- *Too slow; add an index*: an ordinary index makes the lookup faster but does not stop the race; only a uniqueness rule does.

excerpts.quote: In a SQL version, you would need both appropriate unique constraints and transaction handling; a preliminary lookup by itself cannot arbitrate concurrent inserts.

items.title: Why the fix for lost transitions belongs in the model
items.body:
**Key: it keeps the guarantee in the tested domain layer: version expected+1 and the last history entry.**

The solutions chapter offers two fixes. The model fix: in `replay`, treat a repeated `shipment.transition` as already done when the shipment's version is `expected + 1` and its last history entry is the same status and time. The UI fix: on a mismatch, reload and check whether the change is already there. The guide prefers the first because it lives in the domain layer, which is tested, "where this codebase puts every other guarantee".

Why the others are wrong:
- *The UI fix cannot be built*: the guide calls it a reasonable fix; it is just weaker.
- *Adds a requestKey to every transition*: the guide says "no new field needed": version and history already identify the transition.
- *The UI fix is preferred*: the guide says the opposite, and nothing suggests reserve replay would break.

excerpts.quote: In `replay`, for `shipment.transition`, return the state when the shipment's version is `expected + 1` and its last history entry equals `{ status: c.status, at: c.at }`. That is the transition's natural fingerprint; no new field needed.
The first keeps the guarantee in the tested domain layer, which is where this codebase puts every other guarantee.

items.title: Exercise 3's check: red, then green, no fixture changed
items.body:
**Key: "Red first (# fail 1), then # pass equals # tests with no other test changed. The seed subscriber has no overlapping tags ...".**

This is a goal-check question: the practice guide gives each exercise a **Goal** and a **Check**, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

This goal is Exercise 3: add a rule that one tag cannot be both preferred and blocked, without weakening the existing per-field checks. The check is a normal red-to-green loop, plus one detail that matters: unlike Exercise 2, no existing fixture should need editing, because the seed subscriber has no overlap. If an old test breaks, your rule is probably wrong.

Why the others do not fit:
- *"New tests prove: blank is valid ..."*: Exercise 6, delivery notes.
- *Opening balance + movements*: Exercise 7, the ledger.
- *"# tests 37, # fail 1 ... adjusting that fixture"*: Exercise 2, where a fixture *does* break, which is the opposite of this check.

excerpts.quote: **Goal.** Add a cross-field rule to `validateSubscriber` without weakening existing per-field rules.
The seed subscriber has no overlapping tags, so no fixture should need editing.

readMore.why: The solution code: compare case-folded tags after both tags() calls.

items.title: Exercise 5's check: a characterization test that passes today
items.body:
**Key: "The characterization test passes on the current code (# pass equals # tests). If you implement a fix, flip the second assertion ...".**

This is a goal-check question: the practice guide gives each exercise a **Goal** and a **Check**, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

This goal is Exercise 5: find where the idempotency guarantee stops. A *characterization test* records what the code does today, even when that behaviour is a weakness. So it must pass on the current code: the retry of a transition fails with "another tab". If you then fix replay for transitions, you flip that assertion to expect success.

Why the others do not fit:
- *"New tests prove: blank is valid ..."*: Exercise 6, delivery notes.
- *HTTP tests with 401/201/409*: Exercise 9, the server project.
- *Opening balance + movements*: Exercise 7, the ledger.

None of them involves a lost acknowledgement or a retry.

excerpts.quote: **Goal.** Find the boundary of the idempotency guarantee.
await assert.rejects(f.repo.commit(base, command), /another tab/);
**Check.** The characterization test passes on the current code (`# pass` equals `# tests`).

items.title: Exercise 4's check: one assertion, then explain it
items.body:
**Key: "The suite still passes with the new assertion. Then write two sentences: why the loser never reaches the stock check ...".**

This is a goal-check question: the practice guide gives each exercise a **Goal** and a **Check**, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

This goal is Exercise 4: learn what the concurrency control really decides. You add one assertion that the losing request's message matches `/another tab/`. The code is not changed, so the suite must still pass. The second half is understanding: explain why the loser fails the baseline comparison before stock is looked at, and what that means for two people editing unrelated records.

Why the others do not fit:
- *Break the cycle assertion on purpose*: Exercise 8.
- *"# tests 37, # fail 1 ..."*: Exercise 2.
- *Opening balance + movements*: Exercise 7.

Each of those changes the code; this exercise only adds an assertion and an explanation.

excerpts.quote: **Goal.** Learn what the repository's concurrency control actually arbitrates.
assert.match(results.find((r) => r.status === "rejected").reason.message, /another tab/);

readMore.why: Concurrency control is whole-workspace: the section the check points you to.

items.title: A skip and a reserve must fight over one slot
items.body:
**Key: skip racing a reserve for the same month; both must go through one subscriber-month slot.**

A skip says "no box this month"; a reserve says "a box this month". If one client skips while another reserves at the same moment, and each checks a different place (say, a skip flag and the shipments table), both checks can pass and both writes succeed: the month is skipped and shipped. The fix is to give the subscriber-month one authoritative slot with an explicit state (available, skipped, reserved) and a transactional or unique-constraint guard, so only one side can win.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Two skips; disable the button*: UI state does not stop a second client, and the guide warns against keeping skip state in a button label.
- *A skip racing a catalog edit*: they touch different data; this is not the critical race.
- *No race, skips do not touch stock*: the conflict is over the month slot, not stock.

excerpts.quote: The critical race is one client skipping while another reserves. Both must use the same authoritative cycle boundary. If each checks a separate table without an appropriate transaction or uniqueness design, both could succeed.
Give a subscriber-month slot an explicit state, such as available, skipped, or reserved

items.title: Old receipts are judged on their own facts, not today's catalog
items.body:
**Key: it checks internal receipt consistency, and today's availability would make old records unreadable.**

A shipment is a record of what was accepted at the time. Validating it means checking that the receipt agrees with itself and its references, not whether the plan could be sold today. If historical validation asked "is this plan still available?", archiving a plan would make last month's shipments fail validation, and the workspace would stop loading. Current availability is only checked for *new* reservations.

Why the others are wrong:
- *It must check it*: that is the confusion the guide warns about.
- *Never validated again*: the whole state, history included, is validated when loaded or imported.
- *Archived plans are deleted*: archiving is a status change; delete guards keep referenced plans so history remains.

excerpts.quote: New reservations evaluate current eligibility. Historical validation checks internal receipt consistency and references, not today's availability. Confusing these checks could make old records unreadable just because a plan was archived.

items.title: Exercise 6's check: a bounded note, a frozen receipt, a migration
items.body:
**Key: "New tests prove: blank is valid; an overlong note fails; a note accepted into a shipment stays unchanged ...".**

This is a goal-check question: the practice guide gives each exercise a **Goal** and a **Check**, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

This goal is Exercise 6: add an optional, length-limited delivery note everywhere (editor, model, seed, backup format, receipt). The matching check tests exactly those parts: blank allowed, too long refused, the shipment's copy does not change when the subscriber's live note changes, and an old-format backup still loads through a migration (needed because `obj()` demands an exact key set).

Why the others do not fit:
- *Red first, no fixture edited*: Exercise 3, the preferred-and-excluded tag rule.
- *Opening balance + movements*: Exercise 7, the stock ledger.
- *The `node -e ... recommendations` command*: Exercise 1, predicting the recommendation order.

excerpts.quote: **Check.** New tests prove: blank is valid; an overlong note fails; a note accepted into a shipment stays unchanged after the subscriber edits it;
`obj()` requires an exact key set (`src/model.js:5-15`), so adding a key changes the import contract

readMore.why: Why the note belongs to two timelines: the live subscriber and the accepted shipment.

items.title: A failed reservation leaves stock exactly as it was
items.body:
**Key: exactly as before, as the reducer works on a clone, and clamping would hide overselling.**

`reduce` changes a copy of the state, not the accepted state. If it throws on the fifth item, the copy is thrown away and nothing is written, so the first four items keep their stock. The tests compare the stored bytes before and after a rejection to prove it. Clamping the fifth item to zero would let the reservation "succeed" with a unit that does not exist; the guide says that hides overselling instead of proving the box was possible.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Four decrements kept, shipment dropped*: that is the half-saved state the single-value design avoids.
- *Saved as partial*: a reservation is all-or-nothing.
- *Fifth set to zero and saved*: that is the clamping the guide rejects.

excerpts.quote: The reducer works on a clone. If the fifth selected item is unavailable, the first four items in the accepted state must remain untouched. The tests compare accepted bytes before and after rejection.
Saving those changes independently could leave a shipment without reserved stock or reduce stock without a shipment.

items.title: Exercise 7's check: opening balance plus movements equals stock
items.body:
**Key: "A test runs reserve → cancel → manual adjustment and asserts, for one item, that opening balance + sum of movements equals `stock` ...".**

This is a goal-check question: the practice guide gives each exercise a **Goal** and a **Check**, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

This goal is Exercise 7: make every change to `stock` explainable by recording movements. The matching check proves exactly that: after a mixed sequence, the opening balance plus all movements adds up to the current `stock`; a rejected reservation leaves no movements; and the ledger has a size limit, like `shipments` does.

Why the others do not fit:
- *The `node -e ... recommendations` command*: Exercise 1, recommendation order.
- *Suite still passes, two sentences*: Exercise 4, the last-unit race.
- *Break the cycle assertion on purpose*: Exercise 8, skip or replace a cycle.

None of them mentions movements, so none can show that stock is explained.

excerpts.quote: **Goal.** Make every change to `stock` explainable.
A rejected reservation (out-of-stock line) leaves no movements.

readMore.why: Why the ledger needs an opening balance and how reserve and cancel should append movements.

items.title: How a change is accepted: reducer, then commit
items.body:
Every change goes through two pieces of code.

**The reducer** (`reduce` in `src/model.js`) takes the current state and one command (for example "reserve this box" or "move this shipment to Packed") and returns the next state. It works on a copy, and it throws an error if any rule is broken. The glossary calls the result a *candidate*: computed, but not yet accepted.

**The commit** (`commit` in `src/repository.js`) decides whether that candidate is saved. It runs inside a browser Web Lock so two tabs cannot write at the same moment. It reads current storage, checks whether this command was already applied (`replay`), compares the stored text with the text this tab started from (the *baseline*), runs the reducer, and writes the result.

Read the five lines of `commit` slowly and write down the order of its checks. Several quizzes turn on which check runs first.

excerpts.quote: | candidate | the next state, computed but not yet accepted |
| reducer | `(state, command) -> state`, pure, the only way state changes | `reduce` |
`commit` in `src/repository.js:11-24` is lock, replay check, base comparison, reduce, write

readMore.why: The glossary: each term (aggregate, baseline, fingerprint, request key, revision, version) with the symbol that implements it.

items.title: A retried Packed transition gets a misleading conflict
items.body:
**Key: a misleading 'Workspace changed in another tab' error: replay only covers reserve commands.**

The first attempt really did save: storage now holds the Packed shipment. The operator retries from the same old snapshot. Inside `commit`, `replay` returns at once because `c.type` is not `"reserve"`. Then the baseline comparison sees that stored text no longer equals the old base (the first attempt changed it) and throws "Workspace changed in another tab", even though no other tab exists and the change is already saved.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Packed twice*: the baseline check throws before `reduce` can run again.
- *Success, every command replayed*: replay's first line excludes non-reserve commands.
- *"transition is not allowed"*: that message comes from `reduce`, which is never reached.

excerpts.quote: if (c.type !== "reserve") return;
After the retry the operator sees "Workspace changed in another tab", although the transition was saved by the first attempt and no other tab exists.

items.title: Exercise 8's check: break the old cycle assertion on purpose

This goal is Exercise 8: change the one-box-per-subscriber-month policy deliberately (a skip, or a replacement shipment). The check then asks for replay safety under one request key, a race test where two different requests for the same slot cannot both win, and no double stock return.

- *Red first, no fixture edited*: Exercise 3, the tag rule.
- *Suite still passes, two sentences*: Exercise 4, the last-unit race.

**Check.** Your change makes that existing assertion fail, and you update it on purpose with a comment naming the new policy.

items.title: Exercise 2's check: red, one fixture breaks, then green
items.body:
**Key: the "# tests 37, # fail 1 ... adjusting that fixture ... # pass 37" check.**

This is a goal-check question: the practice guide gives each exercise a **Goal** and a **Check**, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

This goal is Exercise 2: one full red-to-green loop that also breaks an existing fixture. The matching check has all three stages: the new test fails first (37 tests, 1 fail); after adding the rule the old test "snapshots survive later catalog and subscriber edits" goes red, because its fixture sets a cost above the retail price; after lowering that cost, all 37 pass.

Why the others do not fit:
- *Characterization test passes, then flip the second assertion*: Exercise 5, the lost acknowledgement on a transition.
- *Opening balance + movements equals stock*: Exercise 7, the stock ledger.
- *Suite still passes, then two sentences about the loser*: Exercise 4, the last-unit race.

excerpts.quote: **Check.** Before the fix: `# tests 37`, `# fail 1`. After the rule alone: `not ok ... snapshots survive later catalog and subscriber edits`.
it edits an item's cost to a value above its retail price only to prove that receipts keep the old cost.

items.title: A blocked tag removes the item before any scoring
items.body:
**Key: nowhere: excluded tags are a hard eligibility filter applied before scoring.**

`recommendations` first runs `.filter((i) => eligible(i, subscriber))` and only then computes scores with `.map`. `eligible` returns false when any of the item's tags matches one of the subscriber's blocked tags (case-insensitive). So the item never reaches the scoring step: preferred-tag matches cannot rescue it.

Why the others are wrong:
- *In the middle, rating halved*: there is no halving; the score formula is 10 per preferred tag plus 5 × rating.
- *Near the top*: matches only count for items that passed the filter.
- *At the bottom, points subtracted*: the guide says exclusion "is a hard eligibility rule, not a small score penalty".

excerpts.quote: !item.tags.some((t) => subscriber.blockedTags.some((b) => b.toLowerCase() === t.toLowerCase()), )
return s.items .filter((i) => eligible(i, subscriber)) .map((item) => ({
Exclusion is a hard eligibility rule, not a small score penalty.

items.title: A new ledger cannot explain stock that existed before it
items.body:
**Key: seed stock existed before any movement was recorded, so it needs an opening balance.**

A ledger explains stock as "start value plus every change since". The seed items already have stock when the app starts, and no movement created those units. If you only add up movements, you get the change since the ledger began, not the current number. So the ledger needs an opening balance per item (or an accepted stocktake event that resets the starting point).

Why the others are wrong:
- *Floating-point drift*: stock and quantities are integers; the problem is the missing starting value.
- *Seed is generated by replaying movements*: the seed is a fixed starting state, which is exactly why it has no movements.
- *Cancellations are not recorded*: in the proposed design they are recorded, as positive movements linked to the shipment.

excerpts.quote: Movement totals alone cannot explain existing sample stock unless there is an opening balance.
Cancellation appends matching positive movements linked to that shipment.
